answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB, resource type 'mongoClusters').

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: az cosmosdb mongodb cluster — this is available in the core 'az' CLI under the cosmosdb command group (az cosmosdb). Example to create: az cosmosdb mongodb cluster create -g MyRG -n myCluster --location eastus --sku M30 --admin-username admin --admin-password 'P@ssw0rd!'.

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (e.g. resource myCluster 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters@2024-06-01' = { name: 'myCluster' properties: { sku: { name: 'M30' } } }). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster (or when using the Cosmos account model: azurerm_cosmosdb_account with kind = 'MongoDB'). Example Terraform resource name: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster" "example" { name = "myCluster" location = "eastus" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name sku_name = "M30" }.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: A MongoDB-compatible connection string. Example (TLS required): mongodb://<username>:<password>@mycluster.mongo.documentdb.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myAccount@. Or mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@mycluster.mongo.documentdb.azure.com/?authSource=admin&ssl=true. Common options: ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet (if required by service e.g. globaldb), retryWrites=false (some Azure Mongo endpoints require this), authSource=admin. Port commonly 10255 for Azure-managed Mongo endpoints that route through gateway; standard Mongo port 27017 may be used for direct-connect offerings.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Provisioned by compute sku/tier (named tiers like M10, M30 — billed by vCores/instance size) and by storage used. Historically CosmosDB used Request Units (RUs) but this MongoDB-compatible offering uses Mongo-style compute SKUs (M-series) and per-GB storage billing. There may also be a serverless or burst option on some SKUs, but primary model for production clusters is compute-tier (M#) + storage.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary auth is MongoDB username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 or SCRAM-SHA-256). The service also supports service principals / managed identities via Microsoft Entra ID for management-plane operations (creating clusters, credentials). For data-plane auth using Entra ID, the driver must obtain an OAuth 2.0 access token from Microsoft identity platform and use it where the service accepts it (for example using the SASL mechanism that the provider documents). Typical app pattern: acquire Azure AD access token with scope for the DocumentDB resource, then pass it as the password or use an authMechanism configured for Azure AD in the driver (implementation details vary by driver).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., official Node.js mongodb driver) or Mongoose for Node.js. There is no separate service-specific runtime SDK for the MongoDB data plane — treat it as a MongoDB endpoint and use MongoDB-compatible clients. For management tasks use the Azure management SDKs or az CLI.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Supported vector index types include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. You create a vector index with the MongoDB createIndex syntax for a knn/vector field. Example command (Mongo shell / driver): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine' } });

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is done by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search for richer text indexing and hybrid text+vector ranking, or with the service's built-in vector/text search index if the managed Mongo endpoint exposes a built-in search feature. Typical approach: create text indexes for standard full-text queries, and use Azure Cognitive Search to index the collection for hybrid retrieval + ranking; or use the provider's vector index (HNSW/IVF) alongside Mongo text indexes and combine results in application code.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Service advertises MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Core CRUD, aggregation and transactions are supported, but some server-side features may be limited: server-side JavaScript (db.eval, $where), certain admin commands, and extensions that rely on specific storage-engine behaviour may not be supported. Also some geo/index internals or custom storage-engine options can differ. Expect differences in change-stream semantics and certain rare opcodes.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator for this managed MongoDB service. For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image matching the advertised wire version, e.g. docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7.0. Use port 27017 for local Mongo. If you need feature parity for Azure-specific capabilities, test against the real cluster in a non-prod subscription.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported by the MongoDB driver via collection.watch() if the cluster implements the MongoDB change stream semantics. No special cluster flag is normally required; however some managed offerings require a replica set topology and appropriate user privileges. If using an API that does not implement oplog access (some gateway models), change streams may be unavailable.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The documentdb MCP server (named 'documentdb' in the run environment) provides the agent data-plane tooling for this service. The general Azure MCP server will not provide service-specific inspection tools for documentdb; use the documentdb MCP server for index/plan inspection and helpers.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' was the name of Microsoft's original document database service that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (the SQL API + multiple APIs). The new 'Azure DocumentDB' name as a MongoDB-compatible managed service reuses the DocumentDB branding but is a separate managed MongoDB-compatible offering distinct from the open-source DocumentDB project; it is related to Cosmos DB only in branding/heritage, not necessarily in implementation.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The data-plane speaks the MongoDB wire protocol; the underlying engine is a MongoDB-compatible server implementation managed by Azure. From application code you should use standard MongoDB drivers (no special SDK) — however expect some differences in edge-case server behaviors or unsupported admin-level features. Use standard Mongo APIs (CRUD, aggregation, transactions) — authentication and connection options may require Azure-specific settings (TLS, retryWrites=false, authSource=admin).

answers.question: Which database name will this sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_customer_360_13 for all sample collections and indexes.

answers.question: What environment variable holds the cluster connection string and how will the app read it?
answers.answer: The sample reads the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. In Node.js use: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; and pass it to mongoose.connect(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }). Include a .env.example with a placeholder value but never store the real URI in repo.

answers.question: What collections and indexes does the sample create to support household linking and vector search?
answers.answer: Collections: customers, households, products. Indexes: customers: compound sparse index on { address.normalized: 1, phone: 1, surname: 1 } for matching; customers: text index on name and address fields for text matching; customers: vector index on embedding field (example) created as db.customers.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine' } }); households: unique index on householdId. These will be created by the app at startup if missing.

answers.question: What aggregation endpoints will the sample expose and what pipeline skeletons will they use?
answers.answer: Expose two endpoints: GET /households/:id/clv — aggregates lifetime value across household members using pipeline: match householdId -> lookup customers by memberId -> unwind products array -> group to sum revenue. GET /households/:id/product-holdings — pipeline: match householdId -> lookup customers -> unwind products -> group by productId to count distinct members and sum quantities. Use Mongoose aggregate([...]) to run these pipelines.

answers.question: Which client library and connection options will the sample code use?
answers.answer: Use Mongoose (npm package mongoose). Connect with: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }); Ensure retryWrites=false is present in the URI if required by the service; use authSource=admin if username/password auth is used.
